cases.answer: In Guo et al.'s source-masked evaluation, the 144 conversational-agent (CA) responses and 144 clinician responses (288 responses, 864 ratings, each rated by 3 clinicians) were compared on overall quality (1-5 scale). CA responses scored higher: mean 4.37 (SD 0.57) versus 3.58 (SD 0.90) for clinicians. The mixed-effects mean difference (CA minus clinician) was 0.782 points (95% CI 0.692-0.872; P<.001). The study notes this holds under controlled, vignette-based conditions and does not establish real-world superiority.

The estimate came from linear mixed effects models, with the difference defined as CA minus clinician.

cases.answer: In He et al.'s primary change-from-baseline analysis, the HbA1c estimate for GQD plus metformin versus metformin alone was a mean difference of -1.92 (95% CI -4.43 to 0.59; P = 0.13). It did not demonstrate a reliable additional benefit. The result was not statistically significant, stayed non-significant under alternative correlation assumptions (r = 0.25 and 0.75), and had extreme heterogeneity (I² 99-100%). It was based on only two trials (196 participants), and the certainty was very low. The authors say the data are insufficient to confirm a reliable additional HbA1c effect, and that the non-significant result is not definitive evidence of no effect.

cases.answer:
Lebedeva et al. (a review, Front. Endocrinol. 2026, on zinc, type 2 diabetes and diabetic kidney disease, DKD) report these zinc/HIF-1α mechanisms. Zinc modulates HIF-1α activity, including by inducing its proteasomal degradation. Zinc also inhibits HIF-1α translocation to the nucleus, which prevents DNA binding and target-gene transcription. That may reduce HIF-1α/VEGF signalling and slow fibrosis by decreasing angiogenesis and inflammation. The review also describes zinc activating Nrf2 and metallothioneins (antioxidant effects). The authors hypothesize that zinc deficiency impairs pVHL-mediated HIF-1α degradation, causing persistent HIF-1α stabilization and sustained VEGF, GLUT1 and EPO expression. They state that the precise mechanisms by which zinc deficiency shifts HIF-1α activity are incompletely understood.

The experimental fibrosis evidence is from animal models of DKD. Zinc administration reduced expression of fibrotic markers, tubular EMT and tubulointerstitial fibrosis, via activation of PI3K/AKT/GSK-3β signalling with decreased HIF-1α expression.

It is not a clinical dosing recommendation. The review says the optimal zinc form, dosage and duration for T2DM patients need more precise strategies and are beyond its scope. It also warns that zinc excess or overdose may be harmful, and it concludes only that zinc deficiency may be a biomarker for risk stratification.

cases.answer: The premise is wrong. In Berthoumieux et al.'s primary intention-to-treat analysis, the HbA1c improvement was significant only at 3 months (difference -0.7%, 95% CI -1.4% to -0.1%; P=.03). At 6 months the difference was -0.6% (95% CI -1.4% to 0.2%; -6.9 mmol/mol; P=.12), which was not significant. So the later (6-month) benefit was a lower but non-significant HbA1c reduction. Statistical significance at both visits appears only in a sensitivity analysis excluding participants who never participated in the intervention: -1% at 3 months (P=.01) and -0.8% at 6 months (95% CI -1.6% to -0.02%; P=.046). The 6-month CGM-derived measures were significant: glucose management indicator -0.9%, time in range +14.6%, time above range -14.9%, and mean glucose -36.4 mg/dL.
